definition: Pick apart data, a graph or a situation to show the key features and how they connect, such as the trend in a set of readings and what limits it. Each point should come from the evidence given.
Add short notes to a diagram or graph, such as marking a node, the amplitude or the region of constant velocity, right where it appears.

Work out a number and show the stages that lead to it: the equation, then the substitution. Give the final value with its unit and sensible significant figures, because the working can still earn marks if the answer slips.

Draw a conclusion that follows from the information given, such as a decay mode from a change in proton number or a relationship from a graph. Show the short chain of reasoning, because a bare answer can score nothing.
Give a full account in words of what happens or what is seen, such as the path of a projectile or the results of a scattering experiment. Reasons are not needed unless asked for.
Find the one answer that fits the information, such as a gradient from a graph or a speed from conservation of momentum, with the working that gets you there.
Weigh up a range of arguments or factors on more than one side, such as the benefits and drawbacks of an energy source. Back each point with physics and end with a clear conclusion.

Make an accurate, labelled diagram or graph in pencil, using a ruler for straight lines and plotting points correctly. On a free-body diagram, start each arrow on the body and give it a sensible length, because each force can carry a mark.
Give a sensible approximate value, and show where it comes from, such as rounded data, a stated assumption or a reading from a graph. One significant figure or a power of ten is often enough.
Say why or how, giving reasons or causes. Build a chain with one link per sentence, such as no resultant force, so constant momentum, so a change in velocity.
Pick out the right answer from a set of possibilities, such as the force that provides the centripetal force or the type of decay. Name it clearly; a reason is only needed if asked for.
Give a brief account or summary of the main points, without full detail. One clear point per mark is usually enough.
Give the result you expect, such as what happens to the fringe spacing when the slits move closer. A reason is only needed if the question asks for one.
Set out the steps of a calculation or derivation that reach the given result, with the equation and substitution written out. In a "show that", give one more significant figure than the value stated.
Draw the right general shape, not to scale, with the relevant features labelled, such as the axes, where the curve crosses zero and where it levels off.
Give a short answer, such as a name, value or law, with no working or explanation needed. For a definition or law, include every key word, because a missing condition loses the mark.
Put forward a sensible possible answer, such as a source of error or an improvement to a method, often in an unfamiliar setting. It needs to fit the physics, not to be the only answer.
